parts.problemMd:
A student needs to find the value of x in the formula (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O He uses this apparatus.

![q15b-1-june-2019-1c-qp-edexcel-igcse-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-8-chemical-tests/assets/004-q15b-1-june-2019-1c-qp-edexcel-igcse-chemistry.png)

The hydrated solid decomposes when heated gently. The equation for the reaction is

(NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O —> (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> + xH<sub>2</sub>O

The table shows the student's results.

| mass of empty test tube in g | 22.04 |
|---|---|
| mass of test tube and (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub>.xH<sub>2</sub>O in g | 34.09 |
| mass of test tube and (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> in g | 28.69 |

(i) Calculate the mass of (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> produced by heating.

(1)

mass of (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3 </sub>= .............................. g<sub> </sub>

(ii) Calculate the mass of water produced.

(1)

mass of water = ..................................... g

(iii) Calculate the value of x.

[*M*<sub>*r*</sub> of (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> = 532 and *M*<sub>*r*</sub> of H<sub>2</sub>O = 18]

Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

(4)

Value of x = .....................................
parts.solutionMd:
i) The mass of (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> produced by heating is:

- 6.65 (g);** [1 mark] **

ii) The mass of water produced.

- 5.4(0) (g); **[1 mark] **

iii) To calculate the value of x:

- Moles of (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> = $\frac{6.65}{532}$ **OR **Moles of (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> = 0.0125 **[1 mark] **
- Moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = $\frac{5.40}{18}$ **OR **Moles of H<sub>2</sub>O = 0.3; **[1 mark] **
- x = $\frac{0.3}{0.0125}$;* ***[1 mark] **
- x = 24;** [1 mark] **

**[Total: 6 marks] **

- *You can calculate the value of x by doing an empirical formula type calculation*

  - *You swap:*
  
    - *The elements for the salt ((NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*(SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*3*</sub>*) and water (H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O)*
    - *The atomic masses for relative formula masses*
- *Compounds* |   | (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.Fe<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> | H<sub>2</sub>O |
|---|---|---|
| Value | 6.65 | 5.40 |
| *M*<sub>r</sub> | 532 | 18 |
| $\frac{\mathrm{Value}}{M_{r}}$ | $\frac{6.65}{532}$ = 0.0125 | $\frac{5.40}{18}$ = 0.3 |
| Ratio (divide by the smallest answer) | $\frac{0.0125}{0.0125}$ = 1 | $\frac{0.3}{0.0125}$ = 24 |
- *You now have the ratio of (NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*.Fe*<sub>*2*</sub>*(SO*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*3*</sub>* to H*<sub>*2*</sub>*O *

  - *1 : 24*
- *Therefore, x = 24*

parts.problemMd:
A scientist finds an unlabelled bottle on a shelf.

She thinks the bottle contains a solution of ammonium sulfate, (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>

Describe tests the scientist could do to show that the solution is ammonium sulfate.
parts.solutionMd:
The tests that the scientist could do to show that the solution is ammonium sulfate are:

Test for ammonium ions:

- Add sodium hydroxide (solution) / other hydroxide solution **OR **Warm with sodium hydroxide (solution); **[1 mark]**
- Test the gas with (damp) (red) litmus <u>paper</u> / (damp) universal indicator <u>paper</u>; **[1 mark]**
- Litmus turns blue  / Universal indicator turns blue / purple (if ammonium ions are present); **[1 mark]**

Test for sulfate ions:

- Add (dilute hydrochloric / nitric) acid **OR **Acidify (the solution);** [1 mark]**
- Add barium chloride (solution) / barium nitrate (solution); **[1 mark]**
- A white precipitate forms (if sulfate ions are present); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *You need to know the various chemical tests*
- *The test for the ammonium ion is typically answered poorly*

  - *Lots of students fail to add that it is the gas being tested*
- *The test for the sulfate ion, using barium chloride more often than barium nitrate, is usually answered well*

parts.problemMd:
Ammonium sulfate is often used as a fertiliser.

It is prepared by reacting ammonia (NH<sub>3</sub>) with sulfuric acid (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>).

i) Name the type of reaction that occurs between ammonia and sulfuric acid.

(1)

ii) Write a chemical equation for the reaction of ammonia with sulfuric acid.

(1)

iii) Draw a dot‐and‐cross diagram to show the bonding in a molecule of ammonia.

Show outer electrons only.

(2)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The type of reaction that occurs between ammonia and sulfuric acid is:

- Neutralisation **OR** Acid-base / acid-alkali;** [1 mark]**

ii) The chemical equation for the reaction of ammonia with sulfuric acid is:

2NH<sub>3</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>;** [1 mark] **

iii) The dot‐and‐cross diagram to show the bonding in a molecule of ammonia is:

![Ammonia dot cross diagram](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-8-chemical-tests/assets/003-ammonia-dot-cross-diagram.jpeg)

- 3 bonding pairs (1 pair between nitrogen and each hydrogen); **[1 mark]**
- Rest of the molecule correct; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Sulfuric acid is obviously an acid and ammonia is a base, so they will react in a neutralisation reaction to form ammonium sulfate*
- *To draw the ammonia molecule:*

  - *Nitrogen is in Group 5 so it needs to share 3 electrons to be considered complete*
  - *Place the nitrogen atom in the centre*
  - *Place the 3 hydrogen atoms in the south, east and west positions with shells overlapping*
  - *Add a pair of electrons to each overlap*
  
    - *Remember:** Hydrogen atoms are full / complete with 2 electrons*
  - *Add the lone pair for nitrogen in the north position*
  - *Check that the nitrogen atom now has 8 electrons*

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd: Describe tests the student could do to show that the mixture contains potassium carbonate and potassium iodide.
parts.solutionMd:
The tests that the student could do to show that the mixture contains potassium carbonate and potassium iodide are:

Descriptions to include **six **of the following points:

parts.problemMd:
A technician finds a white solid in an unlabelled beaker. She knows that the solid is one of the following substances:

- potassium chloride
- potassium sulfate
- sodium chloride
- sodium sulfate.

Describe how the technician can use chemical tests to identify the solid in the beaker.
parts.solutionMd:
The technician can use chemical tests to identify the solid in the beaker:

A description that makes reference to the following six points:

Test for cation:

- Do a flame test; **[1 mark] **
- If the flame is yellow then the cation is sodium; **[1 mark]**
- If the flame is lilac then the cation is potassium;** [1 mark] **

Test for anion:

- Dissolve solid in water; **[1 mark]**

**EITHER**

- Add (dilute nitric acid and) aqueous silver nitrate;** [1 mark]**
- If a (white) precipitate forms the anion is chloride / if no precipitate forms then the anion is sulfate; **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- Add (dilute hydrochloric acid and) aqueous barium chloride; **[1 mark]**
- If a (white) precipitate forms the anion is sulfate / if no precipitate forms then the anion is chloride; **[1 mark] **

**[Total: 6 marks] **

- If asked to show how different ionic compounds can be identified, break up the compounds into cations and anions

parts.problemMd:
This question is about ammonium compounds.

The table shows the names and formulae of some ammonium compounds.

| **Name** | Ammonium nitrate | Ammonium carbonate |   |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Formula** | NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> |   | NH<sub>4</sub>Cl |

i) Complete the table by giving the missing information.

(2)

ii) When ammonia reacts with nitric acid, ammonium nitrate is formed.

Write a chemical equation for this reaction.

(1)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The missing information in the table is:

- Ammonium carbonate formula = (NH<sub>4</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**
- NH<sub>4</sub>Cl name = ammonium chloride;** [1 mark]**

ii) The chemical equation for when ammonia reacts with nitric acid to form ammonium nitrate is:

- NH<sub>3</sub> + HNO<sub>3</sub> → NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *The ammonium ion is NH*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>
- *The carbonate ion is CO*<sub>*3*</sub><sup>*2–*</sup>

  - *This means that you need two ammonium ions to balance the 2- charge from the carbonate ion*
  - *Therefore, the formula of ammonium carbonate is (NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*)*<sub>*2*</sub>*CO*<sub>*3*</sub>
- *NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*Cl contains the ammonium / NH*<sub>*4*</sub><sup>*+*</sup>* ion and the chloride / Cl*<sup>*–*</sup>* ion*

  - *Therefore, it is called ammonium chloride*
- *From the question, you know:*

  - *When ammonia reacts with nitric acid, ammonium nitrate is formed*
  
    - *Ammonia + nitric acid → ammonium nitrate *
  - *You are expected to know the formulae of ammonia and nitric acid*
  
    - *Ammonia = NH*<sub>*3*</sub>
    - *Nitric acid = HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>
  - *The formula of ammonium nitrate is NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*NO*<sub>*3*</sub>
  - *So, the chemical equation is:*
  
    - *NH*<sub>*3*</sub>* + HNO*<sub>*3*</sub>* → NH*<sub>*4*</sub>*NO*<sub>*3*</sub>
  - *No balancing is required for this equation*
  
    - *Previous exams have asked the same question using sulfuric acid to form ammonium sulfate*
    - *Although such an equation will need balancing, it was still only worth one mark! *

parts.problemMd:
When ammonium chloride is heated, it undergoes thermal decomposition to form two gaseous products.

Describe the result of testing each product with damp universal indicator paper.
parts.solutionMd:
The results for each gaseous product from the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride are:

- The products are ammonia / NH<sub>3</sub> **AND **Hydrogen chloride / HCl; **[1 mark]**
- Ammonia = (the universal indicator paper) turns blue / purple;** [1 mark]**
- Hydrogen chloride = (the universal indicator paper) turns red; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Thermal decomposition means that the ammonium chloride must be broken down, using heat, into products that can only be formed from the elements in the original ammonium chloride*

  - *You should also know that ammonium chloride is formed from the reaction of ammonia and hydrochloric acid*
  - *Therefore, you can assume that the reverse reaction is possible*
- *Ammonia is a base, which means that its gas will turn damp universal indicator paper blue / purple*
- *Hydrogen chloride is a strong acid, which means that it will turn damp universal indicator paper red*

> **[exam-tip]**
> Name the gases precisely as ammonia and hydrogen chloride, not 'chlorine', 'chloride' or 'ammonium' — imprecise names lose the mark

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the apparatus used to heat ammonium chloride.

![nh4cl-thermal-decomposition-testing](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/2-inorganic-chemistry/2-8-chemical-tests/assets/002-nh4cl-thermal-decomposition-testing.png)

i) Suggest why the damp litmus paper is two different colours.

(1)

ii) Explain what happens to the damp litmus paper as the ammonium chloride is heated.

(3)
parts.solutionMd:
i) The damp litmus paper is two different colours because:

- Blue litmus paper  **AND **Red litmus paper is being used;** [1 mark]**

ii) Explanation of what happens to the damp litmus paper as the ammonium chloride is heated:

- Ammonia has a lower *M*<sub>r</sub> / mass than hydrogen chloride  **AND  **Therefore, it travels **OR **diffuses quicker / faster; [**1 mark]**
- So, the (damp) red litmus paper will turn blue (first);** [1 mark]**
- The heavier / slower hydrogen chloride then turns both litmus papers red; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

- *Remember:** Litmus paper comes in red and blue to test for alkaline and acidic chemicals respectively *
- *Using both litmus papers suggests that you will be testing for ammonia gas **AND **hydrogen chloride gas*

  - *Many students will incorrectly guess:*
  
    - *That one of the gases turns both litmus papers red / blue and the other has no effect*
    - *That the red litmus paper will turn blue and the blue litmus paper will turn red - this answer suggests that each piece of litmus paper will only be affected by the gas it should be testing for, not the other gas produced*
- *The explanation about colour changes must be linked to the difference between ammonia and hydrogen chloride*

  - *You already know that one is alkaline and the other is acidic but this does not help explain the results*
  - *Ammonia has an **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 14 + (3 x 1) = 17*
  - *Hydrogen chloride has an **M*<sub>*r*</sub>* of 35.5 + 1 = 36.5*
  - *This means that ammonia is lighter and can travel faster*
  - *Therefore, ammonia travels / diffuses quicker and turns the red litmus paper blue*
  - *This means that both litmus papers are blue by the time that the hydrogen chloride gets there*
  - *So, both litmus papers will then turn red*

parts.problemMd: Explain why a fine white powder formed on the inside of the neck of the conical flask in part (c).
parts.solutionMd:
A fine white powder formed on the inside of the neck of the conical flask in part (c) because:

- The ammonia and hydrogen chloride (re)formed ammonium chloride on the cooler / cold surface; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

- *The ammonium chloride decomposes into ammonia and hydrogen chloride when heated*
- *But, ammonium chloride is formed by the reaction of ammonia and hydrogen chloride*
- *So, when the hot ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases lose energy they can react to form ammonium chloride  *

  - *Making contact with a cold surface can cause a suitable energy loss *

parts.problemMd:
The table gives some information about manganese and its compounds.

| Compound | Formula | Appearance |
|---|---|---|
| manganese(II) oxide | MnO | green crystals |
| manganese(IV) oxide | MnO<sub>2</sub> | black powder |

A sample of one of the oxides of manganese contains 63.2 % manganese and 36.8 % oxygen by mass.

Show by calculation that the sample is manganese(IV) oxide, MnO<sub>2</sub>.

[*A*<sub>*r*</sub><sub> </sub>of Mn = 55; *A*<sub>*r*</sub><sub> </sub>of O = 16]
parts.solutionMd:
To show the sample is MnO<sub>2</sub>:

  - O: 36.8% and *A*<sub>r</sub> = 16
- Calculate the moles of each element:

moles = $\frac{mass \left(\%\right)}{M_{r}}$

moles Mn = $\frac{63.2}{55}$

**AND**

moles O = $\frac{36.8}{16}$

**[1 mark]**

moles Mn = 1.15

**AND**

moles O = 2.3

**[1 mark]**

Mn = $\frac{1.15}{1.15}$ = 1

**AND**

O = $\frac{2.3}{1.15}$ = 2

So, the ratio is **1Mn : 2O**

**[1 mark]**

- Therefore, the empirical formula is MnO<sub>2</sub>

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> 1 mark for moles of Mn **AND** moles of OCorrect calculation

> 1 mark for dividing the previous result by the lowest to obtain the ratio

> **[exam-tip]**

parts.problemMd:
Which is true about chemical energy changes?

|   | ** Reaction type** | **Energy flows** | **Temperature of surroundings** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A** | exothermic | to the surroundings | increases |
| **B** | exothermic | from the surroundings | decreases |
| **C** | endothermic | to the surroundings | decreases |
| **D** | endothermic | from the surroundings | increases |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- In an exothermic reaction the energy transferred from the reacting chemicals heats up the surroundings and results in a rise in temperature
- B is incorrect as the energy flow and temperature change are the wrong way around for an exothermic reaction
- C is incorrect as the energy flow is the wrong way around for an endothermic reaction
- D is incorrect as the temperature change is the wrong away around

parts.problemMd: Which statement is **true **about exothermic and endothermic reactions?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is B**

- In an endothermic reaction energy is taken in from the surroundings so that the products have a higher energy than the reactants
- A is incorrect as an exothermic reaction gives out heat energy, so the products are lower in energy than the reactants
- C is incorrect as there is no reason for activation energy to be higher in exothermic reactions than endothermic reactions
- D is incorrect as most reactions are exothermic. The products have less energy and are more stable than the reactants, which is the driving force behind most reactions

parts.solutionMd:
The changes in electronic configuration when lithium and oxygen react to form lithium oxide, Li<sub>2</sub>O are:

- Two lithium atoms each lose one electron / give one electron to oxygen; **[1 mark]**
- Oxygen gains two electrons; **[1 mark]**
- Lithium (ion) has an electron configuration of 2 **AND** Oxide (ion) is 2,8; **[1 mark]** *All 3 marks can be scored from diagrams showing the electron configuration of the ions*

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *An atom of lithium has an atomic number of 3, therefore it has 3 electrons in total*

  - *Its electronic configuration is 2,1*
  - *When it loses its outer electron, it has just 2 electrons remaining, which gives it the electron configuration of 2*
- *Oxygen has the atomic number of 8 so it has a total of 8 electrons *

  - *Its electronic configuration is 2,6*
  - *When it gains 2 electrons to form the oxide ion, its outer shell becomes full and its electronic configuration becomes 2,8*
- *Careful**: Lithium oxide is an ionic compound between a metal and a non-metal, so the electrons are transferred from the metal to the non-metal*

  - *If you make any reference to the atoms sharing electrons, you will be awarded 0 marks*

parts.solutionMd:

parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
During the Second World War, engineers developed a rocket-powered aircraft. ![2c-q51](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-1-energetics/assets/013-2c-q51.png) The aircraft carried these two liquids - hydrazine, N2H4 - hydrogen peroxide, H2O2 When these two liquids mix in the combustion chamber, they evaporate and then react rapidly to form nitrogen gas, N2, and steam, H2O The reaction is exothermic. The equation for the reaction is N2H4 + 2H2O2 → N2 + 4H2O The displayed formulae for the reactants and products are ![2c-q52](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-1-energetics/assets/014-2c-q52.png) The tables give the bond energies for the bonds broken in the reactants and the bonds made in the products. | **Bonds broken ** | | **Bonds made** | | |---|---|---|---| | bond | bond energy

in kJ/mol | bond | bond energy

in kJ/mol | | N—N | 159 | N$\equiv$N | 945 | | N—H | 391 | | | | O—O | 143 | O—H | 463 | | O—H | 463 | | | i) Use the data in the tables to calculate the total amount of energy required to break all of the bonds in the reactants. (1) energy required = .............................................................. kJ ii) Use the data in the tables to calculate the total amount of energy released when all of the bonds in the products are made. (1) energy released = .............................................................. kJ iii) Calculate the enthalpy change, ∆*H*, in kJ/mol, for the reaction. Include a sign in your answer. (3) ∆H = .............................................................. kJ/mol
parts.solutionMd:
i)  Calculating the total amount of energy required to break all of the bonds in the reactants:

- 3861(kJ); **[1 mark]**

ii)  Calculating the total amount of energy released when all of the bonds in the products are made:

- 4649 (kJ); **[1 mark]**

iii) Calculating the enthalpy change, ∆*H*, in kJ/mol, for the reaction:

- 3861-4649 (kJ/mol); **[1 mark]**
- -788; **[2 marks]**

**[Total: 5 marks]**

- *You would score the full three marks for a final answer of -788, but only two marks if your final answer is 788*
- *To calculate the sum of the bonds broken the workings are:*

> *(N-N) x 1 = 159 x 1 = 159*

> *(N-H) x 4 = 391 x 4 = 1564*

> *(O-O) x 2 = 143 x 2 = 286*

> *(O-H) x 4 = 463 x 4 = 1852*

> *    Bonds broken, total = 3861*

- *To calculate the sum of the bonds made the workings are:*

> *(N≡N) x 1 = 945 x 1 = 945*

> *(O-H) x 8 = 463 x 8 = 3704*

> * Bonds made, total = 4649*

- *Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds made)= 3861 - 4649 = -788*
- *There is more energy given out when the bonds are formed than was taken in to break the bonds, so the reaction is exothermic and should have a negative sign in front of the value*

parts.problemMd:
Chlorine reacts with methane in sunlight.

CH<sub>4</sub> + Cl<sub>2  </sub>→ CH<sub>3</sub>Cl + HCl

The diagram below shows the displayed formulae for the reaction of chlorine with methane.

![3-1-q9-edexcel-igcse-chemistry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-1-energetics/assets/020-3-1-q9-edexcel-igcse-chemistry.png)

The table below shows the bond energies and the overall energy change in the reaction.

|   | **C-H** | **Cl-Cl** | **C-Cl** | **H-Cl** | **Overall energy change** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Energy in kJ/mol** | 413 | 243 | X | 432 | -122 |

What is the value of X?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The value of X is 346 kJ
- **Step 1: **Write out the overall bond energy calculation:

overall energy change = Σ(energy needed to break bonds) -Σ(energy transferred to surroundings)

- **Step 2: **Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds

energy need to break bonds = (4 x C-H) + ( 1 x Cl-Cl)

= (4 x 413) + 243 = 1895 kJ

- **Step 3: **Calculate the energy transferred to the surroundings:

energy transferred to surroundings= (3 x C-H) + (1 x C-Cl) + (1 x H-Cl)

= ( 3 x 413) + X + 432 = (1671 + X) kJ

- **Step 4**: Rearrange to find the unknown value:

-122 = 1895 - (1671+X)

1671 + X = 2017

X = **346 kJ**

> i)  You need to know the colours associated with the key substances:
> 
> - Copper(II) sulfate solution is **blue **because of the aqueous Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions.
> - Solid copper metal is a **pink-brown** solid.
> - Zinc sulfate solution is **colourless**.
> 
> The observations describe the blue solution fading as the Cu<sup>2+</sup> ions are replaced, and the pink-brown solid appearing as copper metal is formed.
> 
> ii) Zinc is more reactive than copper, which means that it can displace the copper from its salt solution. This reaction is a metal displacement reaction.
> 
> It is also a redox reaction, as the zinc is oxidised and the copper ions are reduced.

parts.problemMd:
A student investigates the reaction between hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide.

The equation for the reaction is:

HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H<sub>2</sub>O

This is her method.

- Add exactly 25.0 cm<sup>3</sup> of 1 mol/dm<sup>3 </sup>sodium hydroxide solution to a polystyrene cup
- Record the temperature of the solution
- Add 30 cm<sup>3 </sup>of 1 mol/dm<sup>3 </sup>hydrochloric acid and stir the mixture
- Record the highest temperature reached

i) State the type the reaction taking place between an acid and a base.

[1]

ii) State a reason for using a polystyrene cup.

[1]

iii) Suggest why the student used more hydrochloric acid than sodium hydroxide solution.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The type of reaction taking place is:
> 
> - Neutralisation  **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) A reason for using a polystyrene cup is:
> 
> - Polystyrene is an insulator
> **OR**
> It reduces heat loss to the surroundings** [1 mark]**
> 
> iii) There is more hydrochloric acid than sodium hydroxide solution:
> 
> - To ensure all the sodium hydroxide is used up / reacted** [1 mark]** **OR** To make sodium hydroxide is a limiting reagent ** [1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Polystyrene is used for calorimetry experiments because it is a good insulator. This is important to **reduce heat loss** to the surroundings, which makes the measured temperature change more accurate.
> 
> When you want to measure the energy change for a specific amount of one reactant, you must make sure that reactant gets completely used up. The easiest way to do this is by adding an **excess** of the other reactant. In this case, the acid is in excess to ensure all the alkali reacts.

parts.problemMd:
The student recorded the following results:

| volume of<sup> </sup>sodium hydroxide solution in cm<sup>3</sup> | 25.0 |
|---|---|
| initial temperature in <sup>o</sup>C | 18.0 |
| final temperature in <sup>o</sup>C | 24.2 |

i) Show that the heat energy change (*Q*) is about 1425 J.

[for the solution, c = 4.18 J/g/°C]

[mass of 1.00 cm<sup>3</sup> of solution = 1.00 g]

[3]

ii) Calculate the number of moles of sodium hydroxide reacted.

[1]

iii) Calculate the value of the enthalpy change (ΔH), in kilojoules per mole, for the reaction between sodium hydroxide and hydrochloric acid.

Include a sign in your answer.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) To show that the heat energy change (Q) is about 1425J:

- Calculate the temperature change:

temperature change, Δ*T**** ***= final temperature - initial temperature

temperature change, Δ*T**** ***= 24.2 - 18.0

temperature change, Δ*T**** ***= 6.2<sup> o</sup>C**  [1 mark]**

- Calculate the energy change:

*Q *= *mc*Δ*T**** ***

*Q *= 55.0 x 4.18 x 6.2** [1 mark]**

*Q* = **1425.38 J/mol** **[1 mark]**

ii) The number of moles of sodium hydroxide reacted is:

moles = concentration x volume in dm<sup>3</sup>

moles of NaOH = $1.0\times\frac{25.0}{1000}$

moles of NaOH= **0.025 mol** **[1 mark]**

iii) The value of the enthalpy change (Δ*H*), in kilojoules per mole:

molar enthalpy change, Δ*H* =$\frac{Q}{n}$

Δ*H* = $\frac{Q}{n}$= $\frac{1425.38}{0.025}$**[1 mark]**

Δ*H* = -57015.2 J/mol

Δ*H* = **-57.0 kJ/mol ****[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for mass, *m* = 55.0 g **AND **temperature change, Δ*T**** ***= 6.2<sup> o</sup>C
> 
> 1 mark for substitution into *Q* = *mc*Δ*T*** **
> 
> 1 mark for the final answer of 1425.38 J/mol

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> - Moles of NaOH =** **0.025 mol **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii)
> 
> - Substitution into Δ*H* = $\frac{Q}{n}$ **[1 mark]**
> - A value of 57 kJ/mol **[1 mark]**
> - A negative sign **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiner reports highlight several common errors in these calculations:
> 
> 1. **Mass (m)**
> 
>   - Remember that '*m*' in *Q *= *mc*Δ*T* is the total mass of the final solution (acid + alkali), not just the volume of one of the reactants.
> 2. **Unit conversion**
> 
>   - The question asks for the final answer in **kJ/mol**.
>   - So, don't forget to divide your answer in J/mol by 1000.
> 3. **The sign**
> 
>   - For an **exothermic** reaction (temperature increases), the Δ*H* value must be **negative**.
>   - For an **endothermic** reaction (temperature decreases), Δ*H* is **positive**.
>   - Forgetting the sign will lose you a mark.
> 4. Part iii) The question asks for kilojoules, so you must do the conversion at the end, or you will lose the mark. One mark is for the value, and one mark is for the sign.

Example calculation:

Δ*H *in J/mol = $\frac{q}{\mathrm{mols}}$ = $\frac{1600}{0.040}$ = 40 000 J/mol

Δ*H *in kJ/mol = $\frac{40000}{1000}$= −40 (kJ/mol) (negative value for exothermic reaction)

(Q =) 1092

iii) To calculate the enthalpy change (Δ*H*) in kJ/mol, for 1.0 mol of potassium hydroxide:

**[Total: 8 marks]**** **

parts.problemMd:
A student investigates the temperature change during the reaction between zinc metal and copper(II) sulfate solution.

The student considers two different methods.

**Method 1**

![uAvDTga__displacement-calorimetry-exp1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-1-energetics/assets/008-uavdtga-displacement-calorimetry-exp1.png)

- Pour 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of copper(II) sulfate solution into the polystyrene cup
- Record the temperature of the solution
- Add 3 g of zinc powder
- Stir using the thermometer and record the highest temperature reached

**Method 2**

![wjuS5Jtt_displacement-calorimetry-exp2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-1-energetics/assets/009-wjus5jtt-displacement-calorimetry-exp2.png)

- Record the temperature of 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of copper(II) sulfate solution
- Pour the 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of copper(II) sulfate solution into the glass bottle
- Add 3 g of zinc powder
- Push the bung and thermometer into the bottle and record the highest temperature reached

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each method.
parts.solutionMd:
The advantages and disadvantages of each method are:

Any **six **of the following:

**Method 1**:

- Polystyrene (is an insulator so) reduces / prevents heat loss (to the surroundings); **[1 mark]**
- The lack of a lid means that heat / thermal energy will be lost (to the surroundings); **[1 mark]**
- Stirring will ensure an even temperature / more accurate (highest) temperature in the solution 
**OR **
Stirring spreads the heat energy more evenly throughout the solution; **[1 mark]**
- The lack of a lid means that there is a possibility of spillage 
**OR **
The polystyrene cup (containing the thermometer) is unstable / may fall over; **[1 mark]**

**Method 2**:

- The glass bottle is a poor insulator so heat / thermal energy will be lost (to the surroundings); **[1 mark]**
- The bung helps reduce / prevent the loss of heat / thermal energy (to the surroundings); **[1 mark]**
- The bung reduces / prevents spillage; **[1 mark]**
- It cannot be stirred so you cannot ensure an even temperature / cannot ensure an accurate (highest) temperature 
**OR **
The heat energy is not evenly spread throughout the solution; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *This experiment is using calorimetry as a measure of a metal displacement reaction*
- *Therefore, you should be thinking about the advantages and disadvantages in terms of potential energy losses and / or getting the most accurate results*
- *This will include:*

  - *Material choices for the containers, e.g. polystyrene is a better insulator than glass*
  - *Lids to reduce the heat lost from the top of the experiment*
  - *Whether the experiment is stirred or not as this spreads the heat energy more evenly throughout the reaction mixture / solution*

parts.problemMd:
The equation for the reaction is

Zn (s) + CuSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) → ZnSO<sub>4</sub> (aq) + Cu (s)

50cm<sup>3</sup> of copper(II) sulfate solution contains 0.025 mol CuSO<sub>4</sub>

A mass of 3 g of zinc is used.

Show that the zinc is in excess.

[*A*<sub>r</sub> of zinc = 65]
parts.solutionMd:
To show that the zinc is in excess:

Method 1:

- 0.025 moles of CuSO<sub>4</sub> reacts with 0.025 moles of Zn; **[1 mark]**
- So, the mass of Zn needed = 0.025 x 65 = 1.625 g (which is less then 3 g, therefore, the zinc is in excess); **[1 mark]**

Method 2:

- 0.025 moles of CuSO<sub>4</sub> reacts with 0.025 moles of Zn; **[1 mark]**
- 3 g of Zn = $\frac{3}{65}$ = 0.046 moles (which is more than 0.025, therefore, the zinc is in excess); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Tip: **State the molar relationship of the chemicals in question as this is often worth a mark *
- *Limiting reagent and reagent in excess questions will require you to work out the mass of a reagent (method 1) or the number of moles of a reagent (method 2)*
- *The values calculated then allow you to compare against the amount of chemical used  *

parts.problemMd:
The student reacts a solution containing 0.025 mol CuSO<sub>4</sub> with an excess of zinc.

These are the student’s results.

- Temperature of 50 cm<sup>3</sup> of copper(II) sulfate solution = 21.1 °C
- Highest temperature reached = 40.6 °C

i) Show that the energy change Q for this reaction is about 4000 J

[mass of 1 cm<sup>3</sup> of solution = 1.0 g]

[for the solution, c = 4.2 J / g / °C]

(3)

ii) Calculate the molar enthalpy change (Δ*H*), in kJ / mol, for the reaction.

(3)

Δ*H* = .............................. kJ / mol
parts.solutionMd:
i) To show that the energy change Q for this reaction is about 4000 J:

- Temperature rise = 40.6 - 21.1 
**OR **
Temperature rise = 19.5; **[1 mark]**
- Q = 50 x 4.2 x 19.5; **[1 mark]**
- Q = 4095 (J) 
**OR **
Q = 4100 (J); **[1 mark]** 
*The sign written with this answer is ignored*

ii) The molar enthalpy change (Δ*H*), in kJ / mol, for the reaction is:

- Molar enthalpy change in J = $\frac{4095}{0.025}$; **[1 mark]**
- Molar enthalpy change in J = 163,800; **[1 mark] **
*Rounded values are accepted, e.g. 164,000 and 160,000*
- Conversion to kJ with correct sign = -163.8; **[1 mark] **
*Rounded values are accepted, e.g. -164 and -160*

**[Total: 6 marks]**

- *This question is a good example of the steps required to complete a molar enthalpy change calculation*

  1. *Calculate the temperature change of the reaction*
  
    - *A surprising number of candidates will guess at the calculation using one of the given temperatures, rather than calculate the temperature change*
  2. *Use that value to calculate the heat energy change, Q*
  
    - *The most common mistake in this step is to use an incorrect value for the mass, m*
  3. *Divide Q by the number of moles to calculate the molar enthalpy change*
  4. *Convert the molar enthalpy change from J / mol to kJ / mol by dividing by 1000*
  
    - *This conversion is often forgotten by exam candidates or completed incorrectly, e.g. ÷100 or x 1000*

parts.problemMd:
The ionic equation for the reaction is

Zn (s) + Cu<sup>2+</sup> (aq) → Zn<sup>2+</sup> (aq) + Cu (s)

Explain what is oxidised and what is reduced in this reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
Explanation of what is oxidised and what is reduced in this reaction:

Alternative 1:

- Zinc / Zn is oxidised because it loses electrons; **[1 mark]**
- Copper <u>ions</u> / Cu<sup>2+</sup> are reduced because it gains electrons; **[1 mark]**

Alternative 2:

- Zinc / Zn is oxidised 
**AND **
Copper <u>ions</u> / Cu<sup>2+</sup> are reduced; **[1 mark]**
- Because the zinc transfers / loses electrons to the copper ions / Cu<sup>2+</sup>; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *Remember:** OIL-RIG - oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons*

  - *The copper ions / Cu*<sup>*2+*</sup>* will gain 2 negative electrons to become copper atoms*
  - *At the same time, the zinc atoms will lose 2 electrons to become zinc ions / Zn*<sup>*2+*</sup>* *
- *Careful: **Examiners are strict about the use of the words atoms and ions*

  - *For example, if you said that zinc is oxidised because it loses electrons while copper is reduced because it gains electrons, you would lose the second mark for talking about copper and not specifying copper ions*
  - *Tip: **The best way to get around this issue it to use the chemical symbols*

parts.problemMd:
How much energy is needed to break all the bonds in 0.025 g of nitrogen gas?

The relative atomic mass, *Ar*, of N is 14.

| **Bond** | ** Bond energy in kJ/mol** |
|---|---|
| N$\equiv$N | 945 |
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C because**

- **Step 1: **Calculate the amount of nitrogen present

$\mathrm{moles}=\frac{\mathrm{mass} \mathrm{in}g}{\mathrm{molar} \mathrm{mass} \mathrm{in}g/\mathrm{mol}}$

$\mathrm{moles} \mathrm{of}N_{2}=\frac{0.025g}{28.0g/\mathrm{mol}}$

= 8.93 x 10<sup>-4 </sup>mol

- **Step 2: **Calculate the energy needed to break the bonds and convert to Joules:

energy needed = moles x bond energy

= 8.93 x 10<sup>-4 </sup>x 945 = 0.844 kJ

= 0.844 kJ  $\times$ 1000 = 844 J

*Remember this is for nitrogen molecules, N<sub>2</sub>, not atoms

parts.problemMd:
A car manufacturer claims a car model consumes 56 miles per gallon of petrol (gasoline).

When a kilogram of gasoline is burned, 5.3 x 10<sup>5</sup> kJ of heat energy is produced.

(1 gallon = 4.54 litres)

i) Calculate how many miles per litre the car consumes.

[1]

ii) Calculate the heat energy change, in kJ/mol, produced by the fuel.

You should assume the gasoline is pure octane, C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>.

Give your answer to three significant figures.

(*M*<sub>r</sub>* *of C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> = 114 )

[3]

iii) The manufacturer claims the car can travel 650 miles on a full tank of petrol. Deduce the size of the fuel tank in litres.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The number of miles per litre the car consumes is:

miles per litre = $\frac{\mathrm{miles} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{gallon}}{\mathrm{litres} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{gallon}}$

miles per litre = $\frac{56}{4.54}$

miles per litre =** 12.3 miles/L** **[1 mark]**

ii) The heat energy, in kJ/mol, produced by the fuel is:

- Convert mass into moles:

moles = $\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{M_{r}}$

moles in 1 kg of octane = $\frac{1000g}{114}$

moles in 1 kg of octane = 8.7719 mol **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the energy released per mole:

8.77 moles = 5.3 x 10<sup>5 </sup>kJ heat energy

1 mole = $\frac{(5.3\times10^{5})}{8.7719}$

heat energy = 60420 kJ/mol **[1 mark]**

heat energy = **-60,400 kJ/mol**** ****OR** **-6.04 x10**<sup>**4 **</sup>**kJ/mol** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii)
> 
> - Moles of octane = 8.77 **[1 mark]**
> - Correct calculation of energy per mole = 60433 kJ/mol **[1 mark]**
> - Correct final answer rounded to 3 s.f. **AND** With a negative sign (e.g., -60400 or -6.04x10<sup>4</sup>) **[1 mark]**

iii) The size of the fuel tank is:

size of the fuel tank = $\frac{\mathrm{miles}\times\mathrm{litres}/\mathrm{gallon}}{\mathrm{miles}/\mathrm{gallon}}$

size of the fuel tank = $\frac{650\times4.54}{56}$

size of the fuel tank = **52.7 Litres** **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In multi-step calculations like part (ii), it is important not to round your answer too early. Use the full value from your calculator for the number of moles (8.7719...) in the next step to ensure your final answer is accurate. Only round right at the end to the number of significant figures required.
> 
> Remember that **combustion is always an exothermic reaction**, meaning it releases heat. Therefore, the enthalpy change (ΔH) for combustion must always be given a **negative sign**. Forgetting the sign will lose you a mark.

parts.problemMd:
When the fuel burns, the carbon in the octane turns into carbon dioxide:

2C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> + 25O<sub>2</sub> → 16CO<sub>2   </sub>+  18H<sub>2</sub>O

Calculate the volume of carbon dioxide gas at room temperature and pressure when 1.0 kg of the fuel burns.

[for a gas, molar volume = 24 dm<sup>3</sup> at rtp]
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the volume of carbon dioxide gas (at rtp) when 1.0 kg of the fuel burns:

- Find the moles of octane in 1 kg:

moles of octane = $\frac{1000g}{114}$ = 8.7719 mol

- Determine the moles of CO<sub>2</sub>:

the ratio of C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> to CO<sub>2</sub> is 2 : 16 or 1 : 8

moles of CO<sub>2</sub> = moles of C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> × 8 ** [1 mark]**

moles of CO<sub>2</sub> = 8.7719 × 8

moles of CO<sub>2</sub> = 70.175 mol** [1 mark]**

- Convert the moles of CO₂ into volume.

volume = moles × molar volume

volume of CO<sub>2</sub> = 70.175 × 24 = 1684.2 dm<sup>3</sup>

volume of CO<sub>2</sub> ≈ **1680 dm**<sup>**3**</sup>** (to 3 s.f.) ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Answers between 1680 - 1684 dm<sup>3</sup> would be acceptable.
> 
> Allow error carried forward from an incorrect value for moles in part (a)(ii).
> 
> A correct answer with or without working scores 3 marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> In longer calculation questions, you are often expected to use an answer you calculated in a previous part. Here, you needed the number of moles of octane from part (a)(ii).
> 
> You must use the balanced chemical equation to find the mole ratio between the substance you know (octane) and the substance you want to find out about (carbon dioxide). In this case, the ratio is 2:16, or 1:8.

parts.problemMd:
The data in the table gives some information and bond energies.

| Bond | Bond energy in kJ/mol |
|---|---|
| C-H | 413 |
| O=O | 498 |
| C=O | 805 |
| H-O | 464 |

Use the information to calculate the enthalpy of reaction for the combustion of carbon:

CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> $\rightarrow$CO<sub>2  </sub>+ 2H<sub>2</sub>O
parts.solutionMd:
To calculate the enthalpy of reaction for the combustion of methane:

- Calculate the energy of the bonds broken:

* *4 x* E*(C-H) = 4 x 413=  +1652

*2 x E*(0=0) = 2 x 498 = +996

Bonds broken = +1652 + 996 = +2648 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the energy of the bonds formed:

2 x *E*(C=O) = 2 x (-805) = -1610

4 x *E*(H-O) = 4 x (-464) = -1856

Bonds formed = -1490 + (-1856) = -3466 **[1 mark]**

- Calculate the enthalpy of reaction:

enthalpy of reaction = bonds broken + bonds formed **[1 mark]**

enthalpy of reaction = (+2648) + (-3466)

enthalpy of reaction =** -818 kJ/mol** **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> The correct final answer scores all the marks

> **[exam-tip]**
> When bonds are broken, the reaction is endothermic, and energy is put in, so the sign is positive.
> 
> When bonds are formed, the reaction is exothermic and energy is released, so the sign is negative.
> 
> The enthalpy of reaction is the sum of the bonds broken and formed.
> 
> Watch out for multiples of bonds in molecules; CO<sub>2 </sub>has two C=O bonds, so the bond energy is doubled. The water is tricky; there are two 0-H bonds per molecule, so two H<sub>2</sub>0 molecules would have 4 O-H bonds.

parts.problemMd:
Draw a reaction profile to represent the combustion of carbon, including labels for activation energy and the enthalpy change:

![Chemical reaction diagram with an upward arrow labelled "energy," showing CH₄ + 2O₂ underlined, indicating reactants with energy input.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-1-energetics/assets/001-chemical-reaction-diagram-with-an-upward-arrow-l.png)
parts.solutionMd:
A reaction profile to represent the combustion of carbon is:

![Energy profile diagram for the combustion of methane showing activation energy and enthalpy change. Reactants: CH₄ and 2O₂; Products: CO₂ and 2H₂O.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-1-energetics/assets/002-energy-profile-diagram-for-the-combustion-of-met.png)

**[4 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for the energy level for the products (CO<sub>2 </sub>+ 2H<sub>2</sub>O) drawn **lower** than the energy level for the reactants (CH<sub>4 </sub>+ 2O<sub>2</sub>)
> 
> 1 mark for a curve drawn from the reactants' level, rising to a peak (the 'hump') and then falling to the products' level
> 
> 1 mark for the activation energy (*E*<sub>a</sub>) labelled with an arrow pointing upwards from the reactants' level to the peak of the curve
> 
> 1 mark for the enthalpy change (Δ*H*) labelled with an arrow pointing downwards from the reactants' level to the products' level

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiners say that students often confuse the two primary types of energy diagrams:
> 
> - **Energy level diagrams:** These primarily focus on the relative energy levels of reactants and products, showing the overall enthalpy change (Δ*H*).
> - **Reaction profile diagrams:** These show the energy pathway, explicitly including the energy barrier, or **activation energy** (*Ea*), along with Δ*H*.
> 
> Examiner reports show that students often lose marks on these diagrams for drawing the arrows incorrectly. Remember:
> 
> - **Activation energy (*****E***<sub>**a**</sub>**)**
> 
>   - This is the 'hump' the reactants must get over to start the reaction.
>   - The arrow always goes **from the reactants up to the peak of the curve**.
> - **Enthalpy change (Δ*****H*****)**
> 
>   - This is the overall energy difference between the start and end.
>   - The arrow always goes **from the reactants' level to the products' level**.
>   - For an **exothermic** reaction (like this one), energy is released, so the products are lower and the Δ*H* arrow points **down**
>   - For an **endothermic** reaction, the products would be higher and the Δ*H* arrow would point **up**.

parts.problemMd:
Calcium carbonate reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce calcium chloride, water and carbon dioxide:

CaCO<sub>3</sub> (s) + 2HCl (aq) → CaCl<sub>2</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l) + CO<sub>2</sub> (g)

Which statement is **not** true if the temperature of the reaction decreases?
parts.solutionMd:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C.**

- When the temperature is decreased the particles move more slowly and collide with less energy
- The frequency of collisions decreases
- Fewer particles have the minimum energy to react because the mean energy of particles is lower
- The activation energy remains unchanged by the change in temperature

  - The only way to change the activation energy of a reaction is to use a catalyst which provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy

choices.label: A
choices.textMd: The frequency of the collisions between particles decreases

choices.label: D
choices.textMd: There are fewer particles with the minimum energy to react

Some students investigate the effect of changing the concentration of acid on the rate of this reaction. The diagram shows the apparatus they use.

parts.problemMd:

- Increase the rate of reaction; **[1 mark]**
- (Because) there are more particles in the same volume / closer together; **[1 mark]**

*Ignore "chance" or "probability" of collisions*
*Allow "collisions per second"*
*Max 1 mark if there is any reference to particles moving faster or having more energy (this implies a confusion with temperature)*

- Increase the rate of reaction; **[1 mark]**

**OR**
more frequent successful collisions / more frequent and more successful collisions
**OR**
more frequent collisions between particles having ≥ activation energy; **[1 mark]**
*Requires reference to "successful" collisions or activation energy; "more frequent collisions" alone is insufficient here*
*Allow "More particles have energy ≥ activation energy"*
*Ignore "vibrate more"*

**[Total: 6 marks]**

![energy-level-diagram](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/037-energy-level-diagram.png)
parts.solutionMd:
i) Increasing the pressure increases the rate of this reaction because:

- Particles / molecules are closer together; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore more (successful) collisions per unit time; **[1 mark]**

ii) Using a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction because:

- (A catalyst provides) an alternative pathway; **[1 mark]**
- Of lower activation energy; **[1 mark]**

iii) One other way that the rate of reaction between ethene gas and hydrogen gas can be increased is:

- Increase the temperature; **[1 mark]**

iv) The reaction profile diagram, including labels for the activation energy and the enthalpy change, Δ*H* is:

![completed-reaction-profile](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/038-completed-reaction-profile.png)

- C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> on horizontal line below the reactants; **[1 mark]**
- Activation energy correctly shown and labelled;** [1 mark]**
- Δ*H* correctly shown and labelled; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 8 marks]**

- *It is common for students to get the reaction profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions the wrong way around *
- *Remember: **During an exothermic reaction, energy is transferred to the surroundings so the product will end up with less energy than the reactants*
- *Make sure your lines to demonstrate activation energy and enthalpy change are very clear, as if they look like they stop at the wrong point, the marks may not be awarded*
- *When labelling the activation energy, you should show this as an arrow going from the reactants to the peak of the curve*
- *For Δ**H** you should show an arrow pointing from the reactants to the products*

parts.problemMd:
The reaction between ethene and hydrogen can be represented using displayed formulae.

![calculating-enthapy-change](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/039-calculating-enthapy-change.png)

Use the bond energies in the table to calculate the enthalpy change, Δ*H*, in kJ/mol for this reaction.

Δ*H* = .............................................................. kJ/mol
parts.solutionMd:
The enthalpy change, Δ*H,* in kJ/mol for this reaction is:

- (4 x 412) + 612 + 436 **OR** 2696; **[1 mark]**
- (6 x 412) + 348 **OR** 2820; **[1 mark] ***Ignore sign *
- Δ*H* -124  kJ/mol; **[1 mark]**
 *If M1 and M2 correct* *-124 without working scores 3 *
*(+)124 scores 2 *
*Allow M3 ecf from M1 and M2 *

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Calculate the energy taken in to break the bonds*

  - *(4 x C-H) + (1 x C=C) + (1 x H-H)*
  - *(4 x 412) + (1 x 612) + (1 x 436)*
  - *2696 kJ/mol*
- *Calculate the energy released when new bonds are formed *

  - *(6 x C-H) + (1 x C-C)*
  - *(6 x 412) + (1 x 348)*
  - *2802 kJ/mol*
- *Calculate the enthalpy change by taking the energy released from the energy taken in *

  - *2696 - 2802 = -124 kJ/mol*
  - *A negative answer indicates the reaction is exothermic *
- *If you have miscalculated the energy taken in or the energy released, you can still achieve the third mark if you have correctly taken the values away *
- *Enthalpy change calculations are not hard, but often students complete some of the working out wrong and miss out on full marks so make sure you carefully check your answer once you have finished *

At high temperatures, nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia, NH<sub>3</sub>.

ii) Give a reason why this reaction only occurs at high temperatures.

> 
> - N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> $\rightleftharpoons$ 2NH<sub>3</sub> **[1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The reason the reaction only occurs at high temperatures:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - The reaction has a very high activation energy

> - A lot of energy is needed to break the bonds in the reactants

parts.problemMd:
The rate of the reaction is increased by passing the gases over a catalyst.

Explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction because:
> 
> - The catalyst provides an alternative reaction route/ pathway **[1 mark]**
> - The catalyst lowers the activation energy** [1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is a standard definition you must learn. To get both marks, you must include both parts of the explanation.
> 
> Common mistakes include:
> 
> - Saying "it speeds up the reaction"
> 
>   - This doesn't explain how a catalyst increases the rate of a reaction
> - Incorrectly stating that a catalyst gives particles more energy
> 
>   - A catalyst does not change the energy of the particles
>   - It lowers the energy barrier that the particles need to overcome to react

parts.problemMd: Explain how increasing the pressure of gases increases the rate of reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The reason increasing the pressure of gases increases the rate:
> 
> - The particles / molecules are closer together at higher pressure / more particles in the same volume **[1 mark]**
> - There are more frequent collisions
> **OR**
> There are more collisions per unit time **[1 mark]**
> - There are more frequent successful collisions
> **OR**
> There are more successful collisions per unit time **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> With 'explain' rate questions, build the full chain and don't jump straight to 'more successful collisions' — state the increase in collision frequency first.

parts.problemMd:
Nitrogen is a simple molecule with the formula N<sub>2</sub>.

i) Complete the diagram to show the outer shell electrons in nitrogen.

[2]

![Blank dot-and-cross diagram for a nitrogen molecule](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/009-blank-dot-and-cross-diagram-for-a-nitrogen-molec.png)

ii) The bonds in nitrogen are covalent.

Describe the forces of attraction in a covalent bond.

[2]

ii) Explain why nitrogen has a low boiling point.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The shell diagram for nitrogen is:

![Completed dot-and-cross diagram for a nitrogen molecule, showing three pairs of electrons shared between both atoms and each atom also has a lone pair of electrons.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/010-completed-dot-and-cross-diagram-for-a-nitrogen-m.png)

** [2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) For the shell diagram:
> 
> 1 mark for three shared electron pairs between the nitrogens
> 
> 1 mark for one non-bonding pair on each atom

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) The forces of attraction in a covalent bond are:
> 
> - An (electrostatic) attraction between shared pair(s) of electrons/bonding pairs of electrons **[1 mark]**
> - And the nuclei (of both atoms) **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) Nitrogen has a low boiling point because:
> 
> - The forces between molecules/intermolecular forces (of attraction) are weak **[1 mark]**
> - So, little energy is required to overcome them **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Dot and cross diagrams:
> 
> - These can use dots, crosses, or any combination of dots and crosses that fits the correct electronic configuration.
> - When different elements are present, it can be easier for counting to use dots for one element and crosses for the other.
> - Placing the electrons in pairs is also a good habit that makes it easier to count as well.
> 
> i) Nitrogen is in Group 5, so each atom has 5 outer electrons. To achieve a stable outer shell of 8 electrons, each nitrogen atom must share 3 electrons. So, it forms a triple covalent bond (3 shared pairs) between the atoms. This leaves each atom with 2 non-bonding electrons, which form a lone pair.
> 
> ii) For the definition of a covalent bond, examiner reports show that students often lose a mark for writing "nucleus" (singular) instead of "nuclei" (plural). This is important because the shared electrons are attracted to the **nuclei **of **both **atoms in the bond.
> 
> iii) A common and critical error is to state that "covalent bonds are broken". Covalent bonds are strong and are not broken when a simple substance boils. It is the weak intermolecular forces between the molecules that are overcome.

ii) Write an equation for the reaction.

parts.problemMd:
A student uses this apparatus to investigate the rate of reaction between excess marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid.

ii) Explain what happens to the mass of the flask contents during the reaction.

[2]

iii) Explain how the result of the investigation could change if the experiment were carried out without the cotton wool.

[2]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The equation for the reaction is:
> 
> - CaCO<sub>3</sub> + 2HCl → CaCl<sub>2</sub> + CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O** [1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The mass of the flask:
>

> **[exam-tip]**
> i) A typical mark scheme would allow state symbols. It may ignore them if they are incorrect or missing.
> 
> Make sure to check if the question specifically asks for them.

parts.problemMd:
The graph shows the student's results.

![Graph showing a curve on a grid; y-axis: decrease in mass (g), x-axis: time (minutes), ranging from 0–14 minutes and reaching a decrease of roughly 0.55g.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/007-graph-showing-a-curve-on-a-grid-y-axis-decrease-.png)

Explain the shape of the graph.
parts.solutionMd:
Explaining the shape of the curve:

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **two **pairs from (1 mark per point):
> 
> - The curve is steep(est) at the start **OR **the loss in mass is fastest at the start
> - Because the acid concentration is highest
> 
> **OR **
> 
> - The curve becomes less steep **OR **the loss in mass slows down
> - Because the acid becomes more dilute / less concentrated
> 
> **OR **
> 
> - The curve levels off / becomes flat / plateaus **OR **the loss in mass stops
> - Because the acid has been used up
> 
> **[4 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> For a 4-mark "Explain the shape of the graph" question, you must link the **shape** (the gradient) to the **reason** (the chemistry).
> 
> It is not enough to just describe the shape.
> 
> 1. Steep curve / line:
> 
>   - This implies a fast rate of reaction.
>   - This is due to a high concentration, resulting in frequent collisions.
> 2. Curve gets less steep:
> 
>   - This shows that the rate of reaction is slowing down.
>   - This is because the concentration is decreasing, resulting in less frequent collisions.
> 3. Curve goes flat:
> 
>   - The rate of reaction is zero (the reaction has stopped)
>   - This means that a reactant has been completely used up.
> 
> Examiner reports show that a common mistake is to describe the shape without giving the reasons. So, always use linking words like "because" or "as" to connect your points.

parts.problemMd:
The student repeats the experiment using the same mass of smaller marble chips and the same volume and concentration of acid.

i) On the same grid, draw the shape of the curve obtained.

[2]

ii) Explain the shape of the curve with smaller chips.

[4]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The curve using smaller chips is:

![Graph showing the decrease in mass of chips over time. Two curves are plotted, labelled "smaller chips," with the x-axis in minutes and y-axis in grams.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/008-graph-showing-the-decrease-in-mass-of-chips-over.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> i)
> 
> 1 mark for a steeper curve
> 
> 1 mark for the curve to level out at the same position

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) Explaining the shape of the curve:
> 
> - The curve is steeper than for large chips **[1 mark]**
> - This is because the small chips have a higher surface area **[1 mark]**
> - There a more collisions per unit time **[1 mark]**
> - The curve levels off at the same position as the same amount of acid has been used up **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> i) A sketch of a rate curve must show two things:
> 
> 1. The initial steepness (gradient).
> 2. The final height.

> ii) This is a classic collision theory explanation.  Examiner reports show that to get full marks, you must:

> - Explain its effect on collisions (more **frequent** collisions or more collisions **per unit time**).

parts.problemMd: Explain, using collision theory, how doubling the concentration of the acid affects the rate of reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Doubling the concentration of the acid causes:
> 
> - The rate of reaction to increase/ the reaction to go faster/ the reaction to speed up **[1 mark]**
> 
> Explanation using collision theory:
> 
> Any **two **from (1 mark each):
> 
> - There are more acid particles (per unit volume)
> - There are more collisions per unit time
> - There are more successful collisions
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiner reports show that for a collision theory question about concentration, a high-scoring answer will always include:
> 
> - Particles per unit volume.
> - Collision frequency.
> - Successful collisions.

parts.problemMd:
Zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce zinc chloride and hydrogen.

Complete the chemical equation for the reaction.

.....Zn + ..........HCl → ...................... + ....................
parts.solutionMd:
The chemical equation for the reaction is:

Zn + **2**HCl → **ZnCl**<sub>**2**</sub>** **+ **H**<sub>**2**</sub>** ****[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for 2 before HCl **AND** ZnCl<sub>2</sub> **AND **H<sub>2</sub>

> **[exam-tip]**
> To write this equation, you need to know the chemical formulae for all the substances involved. The trickiest one is zinc chloride.
> 
> You are expected to know the charges on common ions. A zinc ion is Zn<sup>2+</sup> and a chloride ion is Cl<sup>-</sup>. To make a neutral compound, you need two chloride ions for every one zinc ion:
> 
> Zn<sup>2+</sup> + 2Cl<sup>-</sup> → ZnCl<sub>2</sub>
> 
> Once you have the correct formulae, you can balance the equation.

parts.problemMd: Give a test for hydrogen.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> The test for hydrogen is:
> 
> - Place a lighted splint into a test tube of the gas
> **AND**
> It will burn with a 'squeaky pop' **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Examiner reports consistently show that students lose marks by not describing the full test for a gas. For hydrogen, you must state both the **method** and the **result**:
> 
> - **Method:** Use a **lighted** splint
> - **Result:** You hear a **'squeaky pop'**
> 
> Be careful not to confuse this with the test for oxygen, which uses a **glowing** splint.

parts.problemMd:
A student investigates the rate of reaction between zinc and hydrochloric acid.

He uses this apparatus.

![Diagram of an experiment showing zinc reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid in a flask, producing hydrogen gas collected in a syringe.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/001-diagram-of-an-experiment-showing-zinc-reacting-w.png)

The student records the volume of hydrogen that collects every 2 minutes for 16 minutes.

The table shows his results.

| Time in minutes | Volume of hydrogen in cm<sup>3</sup> |

| 0 | 0 |
| 2 | 21 |
| 4 | 39 |
| 6 | 53 |
| 8 | 57 |
| 10 | 73 |
| 12 | 76 |
| 14 | 76 |

(i) Plot the results on the grid.

[1]

(ii) Identify and draw a circle around the anomalous result.

[1]

(iii) Draw a curve of best fit through the points, ignoring the anomalous result.

[1]

![Graph with a grid for plotting volume of hydrogen in cm³ on the y-axis versus time in minutes on the x-axis, both scales marked.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/002-graph-with-a-grid-for-plotting-volume-of-hydroge.png)

The completed graph is:

A point at 8 minutes is circled, indicating 50 cm³.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/003-graph-showing-the-volume-of-hydrogen-in-cm-over-.png)

> i) 1 mark for all points correctly plotted to within <u>+</u> ½ square

>

parts.problemMd: Suggest what could have caused the anomalous result.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Causes of the anomalous result:
> 
> Any **one **from:
> 
> - The barrel of the gas syringe was sticking
> - The student took the reading too soon/ before 8 minutes
> - Some gas escaped from the apparatus before the reading was taken
> 
> **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> When asked to explain an anomalous result, first look at the graph to see if the point is **above** or **below** the line of best fit.
> 
> - The anomalous point in this graph (at 8 minutes) is **below** the curve, meaning the volume of gas recorded was unexpectedly **low**.
> - Your suggested reason must be a practical error that could cause a lower-than-expected reading. For example, taking the reading too early or a sticking syringe would both result in a volume that is too low.
> - Stating that the reading was taken "too late" would lead to a reading that was too high, so that would not be a correct answer for this specific anomaly.

parts.problemMd:

Curved line with marked points; a circled point at 6 minutes, 50 cm³.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/004-graph-showing-hydrogen-volume-in-cm-over-time-in.png)

> 
> Allow error carried forward for an incorrectly drawn curve from part (c)

> **[exam-tip]**
> To show evidence of data read from a graph, you need to show horizontal and vertical tie lines extending to the axes.
> 
> Use a ruler to draw a neat vertical line from the value on the x-axis (5 minutes) up to your curve of best fit. Then draw a horizontal line from that point across to the y-axis to show the value you are reading. This is what examiners call a 'tie line'.

parts.problemMd:
The student repeats the experiment using hydrochloric acid with half the original concentration.

i) On the grid, sketch the curve you would expect the student to obtain.

In your explanation, refer to particle collision theory.

[3]
parts.solutionMd:
i) The curve using half the concentration of acid is:

![Graph showing hydrogen volume in cm³ over time in minutes with two curves; the upper curve has a marked point at 8 minutes and 55 cm³.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-chemistry-19/3-physical-chemistry/3-2-rates-of-reaction/assets/005-graph-showing-hydrogen-volume-in-cm-over-time-in.png)

**[2 marks]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> 1 mark for a curve that starts at the origin and is less steep than the original curve
> 
> 1 mark for a curve that levels off at half the volume in the original experiment (~38cm<sup>3</sup>)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> ii) How halving the concentration of acid affects the reaction rate:
> 
> - There are  fewer particles/molecules (in the same volume)  **[1 mark]**
> - There are fewer collisions per unit time 
> **OR**
> There are less frequent collisions **[1 mark]**
> - So, the rate of  reaction is slower **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> **For the graph:** Remember that changing the concentration of a reactant affects two things:

> 2. **The Amount of Product (the final height):**

>   - Halving the amount of the limiting reactant (the acid) will halve the amount of product formed.

> **For the explanation:** This is a collision theory question. To get full marks, you must link the concepts in the correct order:

parts.problemMd: Explain, in terms of particle collision theory, the effect that increasing the temperature has on the rate of a reaction.
parts.solutionMd:
In terms of particle collision theory, the effect that increasing the temperature has on the rate of a reaction is:

- The (mean) <u>kinetic</u> energy of the particles increases 
**OR **
The particles gain <u>kinetic</u> energy / move faster; **[1 mark] **
*Vibrate more or faster is not accepted*
- This leads to more <u>frequent</u> successful collisions 
**OR  **
This leads to more successful collisions <u>per second / per unit time</u> 
**OR **
This leads to more <u>frequent</u> collisions between particles that have energy greater than the activation energy; **[1 mark] **
*Reference must be made to the frequency of collisions or collisions per unit time to achieve this mark*
- Therefore, the rate (of reaction) increases 
**OR **
The reaction is faster / speeds up; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

- *Most students lose marks on this question because they don't talk about the **kinetic** energy of the particles and the frequency of the collisions*
- *Regardless of the factor (temperature, pressure, concentration or surface area) the reasons that any reaction gets quicker, in terms of collision theory, is:*

  - *There are more frequent collisions / more collisions per unit time*
  - *This leads to more successful collisions*
  
    - *The easiest way to cover both of these points is to say that there are more frequent successful collisions / more successful collisions per unit time*
  - *This causes the rate of reaction to increase*
- *For temperature the additional factor is that a greater number of particles have more energy for collisions to occur with an energy greater than or equal to activation energy at a higher temperature, which further accelerates rate*

Use this equation and the particle collision theory to explain why the rate of reaction is greatest at the start of the reaction.

(3)

iii) The student repeats the experiment at a higher temperature but keeps all other conditions the same. On the grid, draw the curve you would expect to see in this experiment.

i) The mean (average) rate of reaction, in cm<sup>3 </sup>/ s, in the first 120 s is:

- 280 ÷ 120;** [1 mark]**

- The concentration of hydrochloric acid is greatest / greatest number of particles (of zinc / hydrochloric acid)

parts.problemMd:
In another experiment, the student adds 0.55 g of zinc to a solution containing 2.50 × 10<sup>−2</sup> moles of hydrochloric acid. Use the equation to show that hydrochloric acid is in excess.

[*A*<sub>r</sub> of Zn = 65]
parts.solutionMd:
To show that hydrochloric acid is in excess:

- 8.46 × 10<sup>-3</sup> mol of zinc; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore 1.69 × 10<sup>-2</sup> mol hydrochloric acid is needed (which is less than 2.50 × 10<sup>-2</sup> mol); **[1 mark]**

**OR**

- 1.25 × 10<sup>-2</sup> mol of zinc are needed; **[1 mark]**
- Therefore 0.8(13) g of zinc is needed (and there is only 0.55 g); **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 2 marks]**

- *To find which reactant is in excess you need to know the number of moles of each reactant and the reacting ratio*

i)Use this information to calculate the total amount of energy needed to break all the bonds in two moles of H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>.

energy needed = .............................................................. kJ

bond energy = .............................................................. kJ/mol

**OR**

(O=O) = 2144 – 1852 + 204

parts.problemMd:
This question is about reversible reactions and equilibria.

Give two characteristics of a dynamic equilibrium.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Two characteristics of a dynamic equilibrium are:
> 
> - The forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate
> **OR**
> The rate of the forward reaction is equal to the rate of the reverse reaction **[1 mark]**
> - The concentrations of reactants and products remain constant **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two key words to remember for this definition are **"rate"** and **"constant"**.
> 
> - The **rates** of the forward and reverse reactions are **equal**.
> - The **concentrations** of all substances are **constant**.
> 
> A common mistake is to say the concentrations are *equal*, which is incorrect. They are just no longer changing.

parts.problemMd:
Ethanol and ethanoic acid react together in a dynamic equilibrium.

The reaction is exothermic.

The equation for the reaction is:

C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH (aq) + CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (aq) $\rightleftharpoons$ CH<sub>3</sub>COOC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> (aq) + H<sub>2</sub>O (l)

i) Give the name of the organic product

[1]

ii) Predict the effect on the yield of increasing the reaction temperature. Give a reason for your answer.

[2]

iii) The reaction is catalysed by concentrated sulfuric acid. Predict the effect of the catalyst on the reaction yield at equilibrium.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> i) The name of the organic product is:
> 
> - Ethyl ethanoate** [1 mark]**
> 
> ii) The effect of increasing the temperature on the yield is:
> 
> - (The yield) decreases** [1 mark]**
> - An increase in temperature shifts the position of equilibrium in the direction of the endothermic reaction **[1 mark]**
> 
> iii) The effect of the catalyst on the reaction yield at equilibrium is:
> 
> - There is no change in yield as a catalyst does not affect the position of equilibrium in a reversible reaction **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> i) Esters are named according to the alcohol and carboxylic acid used. The naming pattern is **alkyl alkanoate**:
> 
> - The alkyl comes from the alcohol
> 
>   - In this case, **eth**anol, so the group is **ethyl**.
> - The alkanoate comes from the carboxylic acid
> 
>   - In this case **ethan**oic, so the group is **ethan**oate.
> 
> ii) The question tells us that the reaction is exothermic, so the reverse reaction is endothermic.
> 
> - Decreasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the exothermic direction.
> - Increasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium in the endothermic direction.
> 
> So, a shift to the endothermic direction (left in this case) causes a decrease in the yield of products.
> 
> iii) A catalyst has **no effect** on the yield at equilibrium. It only affects the **rate** of reaction, speeding up both the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount.

parts.problemMd:
The reaction to produce sulfur trioxide reaches an equilibrium.

2SO<sub>2</sub> (g) + O<sub>2</sub> (g) $\rightleftharpoons$2SO<sub>3</sub> (g)

The forward reaction is exothermic. The rate of attainment of equilibrium and the equilibrium yield of sulfur trioxide are affected by pressure and temperature.

A manufacturer considered two sets of conditions, A and B, for this reaction.

In each case sulfur dioxide is mixed with excess oxygen.

The manufacturer changed the temperature and the pressure and only used a catalyst in B.

The sets of conditions A and B are shown in Figure 7.

| set of conditions | pressure in atm | temperature in °C | catalyst |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | 2 | 680 | no catalyst used |
| B | 4 | 425 | catalyst used |

**Figure 7**

The manufacturer chooses set of conditions B rather than set of conditions A.

Explain, by considering the effect of changing the conditions on the rate of attainment of equilibrium and on the equilibrium yield of sulfur trioxide, why the manufacturer chooses the set of conditions B rather than the set of conditions A.
parts.solutionMd:
The manufacturer chooses the set of conditions B rather than the set of conditions A because:

Chemical ideas expressed:

**Temperature**:

- The equilibrium is reached faster because of the higher temperature in set A 
**OR **
The equilibrium is reached slower because of the lower temperature in set B
- The higher temperature means that there are more frequent collisions because molecules have more energy in set A 
**OR **
The lower temperature means that there are less frequent collisions because molecules have less energy in set B
- The decrease in temperature increases the equilibrium yield but the system takes longer to reach equilibrium
- The temperature chosen for optimum conditions
- The yield lowers / decreases as the forward reaction is exothermic
- A high temperature favours the backwards reaction, which is endothermic
- The equilibrium is reached faster because of the higher pressure in set B 
**OR **
The equilibrium is reached slower because of the lower pressure in set A

**Pressure:**

- Higher pressure causes molecules to be closer together so there are more frequent collisions in set B 
**OR **
Lower pressure causes molecules to be further apart so there are less frequent collisions in set A
- The yield is higher because the products occupy a smaller volume than reactants for set B

**Catalyst:**

- The catalyst used in set B causes the equilibrium to be reached faster
- A catalyst increases the rate of both forward and backward reactions
- The equilibrium position is not affected so the catalyst does not affect the yield

**Level 1:** **(1−2 marks)**

- A basic answer with some chemical ideas, missing information, using simple language and not presented in a logical order

**Level 2:**** ****(3−4 marks)**

- A relevant answer with confidently expressed chemical ideas, a few details missing and some chemical terms included

**Level 3:** **(5−6 marks)**

- A well developed answer that covers chemical ideas in a detailed and logical way, using a wide range of chemical terms

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> * Level 1 answer could be:*

- *A simple explanation of why B was chosen in terms of 2 conditions*
- *A detailed explanation of why B was chosen in terms of 1 condition but may lack a full explanation*

> *An example of a Level 1 answer scoring 2 marks would be:*

> *A lower temperature is used as the forward reaction is exothermic.  A catalyst speeds up the rate of the reaction.*

- *A simple explanation of why B was chosen in terms of temperature and use of a catalyst (2)*

> *Level 2 answer could be:*

- *A simple explanation of why B was chosen in terms of 3 conditions*
- *A simple explanation of why B was chosen in terms of 1 condition **AND **a detailed explanation in terms of 1 other condition*

> *An example of a Level 2 answer scoring 4 marks would be:*

> *Higher pressure is favoured because the rate of reaction is quicker. A catalyst would not affect the yield but it speeds up the time taken to reach equilibrium as it increases the rate of both the forward and reverse reaction, so it reduces the need for higher temperatures.*

- *A simple explanation of why B was chosen in terms of pressure and** **a detailed explanation in terms of the use of a catalyst (4)*

> *Level 3 answer could be:*

- *A detailed explanation of why B was chosen in terms of 2 or more conditions*

> *An example of a Level 3 answer scoring 6 marks would be:*

> *A lower temperature gives a higher yield because the forward reaction is exothermic, so decreasing the temperature shifts the equilibrium position to the right.*

> *A higher pressure gives a higher yield because there are fewer gas molecules on the product side, so increasing pressure favours the forward reaction.*

> *Although a lower temperature would reduce the rate of reaction, a catalyst is used to speed up the rate and allow equilibrium to be reached more quickly.*

> *So condition B is chosen because it increases both the yield (by favouring the forward reaction) and the rate (due to the catalyst and higher pressure).*

- *A detailed explanation of why B was chosen in terms of temperature and pressure and a simple explanation in terms of a catalyst (6)*
